Sofía Villarreal

gap-003 · supplement · fictional age 16

Written life first, then interpreted by a separate response author without the engine or results. These are synthetic checks. There is no correct career answer key.

Life from age 4 to 16

I like growing things, except the phrase sounds cute and most of it is checking the same stuff again. I like that part too, sometimes. I am not brave about hurt animals. People act like that cancels knowing anything else. I might leave here for school. I might want to come back. I want enough information that it is an actual choice and not everybody arguing about a picture in their head.

  • family: Lives with her parents, grandmother, and two cousins during the school week; relatives share tasks on a small leased growing plot.
  • finances: Income varies by season and parents’ paid work; the family tracks supplies closely.
  • geography: Near Weslaco in the Rio Grande Valley, Texas.
  • cultureLanguages: Spanish and English across home and school; grandmother prefers Spanish.
  • school: Public high school with an agricultural elective; math performance is steady while long reading assignments take more effort.
  • accessOpportunities: Direct experience with vegetables and chickens, borrowed tools, school internet, and limited access to paid camps.
  • Age 4–5

    At four Sofía helped her grandmother wash plastic buckets and made mud soup with a cousin. She loved the chickens until one chased her across the yard. For months she insisted on being carried past their pen, while still demanding to collect the warm eggs after an adult went in.

  • Age 6–7

    At six she kept a row of bean plants in reused cups. Some died because she watered all of them every time she remembered. Her grandmother explained the wet soil, but Sofía mainly wanted a replacement seed. She also liked racing bicycles on the short lane beside the house.

  • Age 8–9

    Between eight and nine she began comparing which plants wilted first. She could recognize several common weeds by sight but mixed up their names at school. At a roadside produce table she liked stacking colors and watching customers choose, although she hid behind her father when asked to make change.

  • Age 10–11

    At ten her father let her enter seed and feed purchases in a ruled notebook. She copied figures accurately when the receipts were legible and sometimes switched columns. Counting the remaining sacks helped her understand the mistake. She enjoyed that there was a physical thing to check against the number.

  • Age 12–13

    At twelve a sick chicken needed to be separated. Sofía helped prepare water and bedding but would not watch an adult examine its injury. She remained interested in eating, growth, and disease prevention without enjoying every part of animal care. Her cousin teased her, which made her refuse to discuss it.

  • Age 14–15

    At fourteen she took an agricultural elective and learned that classmates with similar family experience had very different equipment and free time. A friend posted polished growing videos; Sofía copied a labeling idea but abandoned filming because everyone at home interrupted. Her favorite success was reducing repeated trips for forgotten supplies.

  • Age 16

    Now sixteen she checks a weekly supplies list and can spot when an order exceeds available storage. She enjoys selling produce alongside her father but dislikes bargaining with people who treat her as a child. Her parents hope for a four-year college; she wants more training but has not agreed about distance or cost.

Life now

  • enjoys: Checking plant growth · Arranging produce · Matching records to real stock
  • avoids: Watching open animal wounds · Filming household work · Condescending bargaining
  • activities: Agricultural elective · Weekly supply list · Seasonal produce table
  • demonstratedSkills: Recognizes familiar plant stress signs · Reconciles simple quantities with stock · Plans a workable sequence of errands
  • unfamiliarActivities: Large farm machinery · Advanced accounting · Residential college life
  • motivations: Reducing wasted supplies and trips · Keeping family options open
  • ambitions: Continue learning after high school · Help replace an unreliable irrigation timer
  • struggles: Embarrassment about avoiding injuries · Family disagreement about distance · Long reading tasks
  • supports: Grandmother’s patient explanations · Agricultural teacher · Parents who include her in decisions
  • practicalConstraints: Seasonal work demands · Limited camp funds · Transportation shared among relatives

Still uncertain: Would she enjoy larger systems with less direct contact with plants? · What distance and training arrangements would feel workable to her?

Six scores & initial pathways

R, I, A, S, E, C: 23 / 23 / 20 / 20 / 24 / 31, each out of 40. Interests, not ability or success odds.

Pathways: Sales, office & customer support · Transport & production · Engineering & building

Work-led options: Food, hospitality & personal care · Science & environment · Trades & technical repair

Field explored: science. Sofía chooses plant growth and growing systems because she repeatedly checks plants, watering, supplies, and storage. Her choice preserves a boundary around injuries and does not make animal treatment a necessary part of liking living systems.
